nameStory: The 'clasping' in clasping coneflower comes from how its oval leaves wrap around and clasp the stem at their base, like a gentle hug. The 'coneflower' part describes the prominent dark center that rises up like a little cone above the bright yellow petals, similar to its black-eyed Susan cousins.
description: Clasping coneflower is an annual wildflower that grows up to 3 feet tall with cheerful daisy-like blooms. Its bright yellow petals surround a dark, cone-shaped center that gives the plant its name. The smooth stems can be simple or branched, and the oval leaves have a distinctive way of wrapping around the stem. This plant is actually quite rare in New England, making any sighting a special treat for wildflower enthusiasts.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval leaves 2-4 inches long that clasp and wrap around the stem at their base - run your finger along the stem and feel how the leaf base encircles it completely

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellow daisy-like flowers with a prominent dark brown to purple cone center that feels firm and bumpy to the touch

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Annual plant reaching 3 feet tall with smooth, hairless stems that may branch toward the top

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Ray petals may have a slight yellowish-purple tinge and the dark center has small chaffy scales between the tiny disc flowers

habitat: Clasping coneflower is extremely rare in New England, with only a handful of documented sightings. When found, it typically grows in disturbed soils, field edges, and waste places. It prefers full sun and well-drained soils, often appearing in areas that have been recently cleared or cultivated.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge and develop their characteristic clasping leaves, forming low rosettes before sending up flower stems.
seasonality.summer: Bright yellow flowers bloom from mid to late summer, attracting bees and butterflies to their nectar-rich centers.
seasonality.fall: Seeds mature in the cone-like centers and the plant begins to die back, scattering seeds for next year's generation.
seasonality.winter: As an annual, the plant dies completely, leaving only seeds in the soil to sprout the following spring.

funFact: This plant is so botanically unique that scientists moved it to its own separate genus called Dracopis - it's the only species in that genus in the entire world, making it a true botanical singleton!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with black-eyed Susan, but clasping coneflower's leaves wrap completely around the stem like a collar, while black-eyed Susan's leaves are hairy and don't clasp the stem. Remember: 'clasping' is right in the name - look for that hugging leaf base.
contextualKnowledge: This plant causes confusion even among botanists - it used to be classified as Rudbeckia amplexicaulis but was moved to its own genus Dracopis because of unique flower characteristics. You might see it listed under either name in older field guides.
compareHints: Unlike its Rudbeckia cousins, clasping coneflower has small chaffy scales (like tiny bracts) beneath its ray petals that other black-eyed Susans lack. Its perfectly smooth, clasping leaves also set it apart from the typically hairy, non-clasping leaves of true Rudbeckia species. The plant's annual nature distinguishes it from most perennial coneflowers.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Rudbeckia relatives, black-eyed Susan is distinguished by its rough, hairy texture and moderate size.

Among the Rudbeckia family, cutleaf coneflower is the giant with the fancy haircut - it's much taller than black-eyed Susan and has those distinctive deeply-divided leaves that no other coneflower possesses.
Among the Rudbeckia family, brown-eyed Susan stands out for its smaller flowers and brown (not black) centers.
Orange coneflower differs from black-eyed Susan by forming spreading colonies rather than individual clumps, and has slightly more orange-tinted petals.
Among its Rudbeckia relatives, sweet black-eyed Susan stands out for its impressive height and fragrant flowers.

Great coneflower's towering 8-foot height immediately distinguishes it from all other Rudbeckia species in New England - black-eyed Susan tops out around 3 feet, cutleaf coneflower reaches about 4-6 feet, and orange coneflower stays under 3 feet.
